tip: Swedish uses one verb form for every subject: hon somnar, jag somnar, du somnar. There is no 3rd-person -s like English 'she falls'.
Swedish adds 'the' onto the end of the noun: solnedgång becomes solnedgången = the sunset. There is no separate word for 'the'.
Prata is the everyday word for talk or chat, as in de pratar svenska. Tala means the same but sounds more formal.
Common-gender nouns take -en for 'the': butiken = the shop. Neuter nouns take -et instead, like huset = the house.
Jobba is the casual word for work, as in han jobbar. Arbeta means the same but sounds more formal.
Halv åtta means 7:30, not 8:30. Swedish counts toward the next hour, so it is literally half to eight.
Middag looks like English 'midday' but means dinner, the evening meal, as in vi äter middag klockan sex.
Vill means 'want', not English 'will': jag vill lära mig means I want to learn, not I will learn.
Swedish keeps the verb in second place, so fronting I Sverige puts äter ahead of the subject man: I Sverige äter man.
In a main clause the verb comes before inte: du skämtar inte. In a subordinate clause (att, om, som) it flips to inte before the verb.
The dummy subject stays det är no matter what follows: det är varmt. Learners wrongly reach for den är with en-words.
Det finns means 'there is' for existence: det finns bröd på hyllan. Det är means 'it is', like det är bröd.
The perfect uses har plus the supine: har allt gått bra. The supine gått is a distinct form from the plain past tense.
Bra never changes form: en bra dag, and it stays bra in every position, unlike stor which becomes stort.
In a subordinate clause the subject stays before the verb: då allt förändrades, not då förändrades allt. No verb-second here.
The whole clause Hur vi löser problemet fills the first slot, so the main verb comes next, before its subject: vet jag inte.
In Hur gammal är du, du is the only 'you' Swedish needs, from strangers to bosses. Formal Ni is gone.
A non-subject first element forces the verb second and the subject third: I princip är vi. Same rule as German and Dutch.
Liten is irregular: you say en liten stad, but the plural is små, which looks nothing like liten.
In a subordinate clause inte comes before the verb: så att vi inte missar. Compare the main-clause order verb before inte.
A fronted adverb pushes the verb ahead of the subject: Snart kommer sommaren, not Snart sommaren kommer.
In a main clause inte follows the verb: Det kan inte stämma. Putting inte first is wrong.
Sju (seven) starts with the sj-sound written [ɧ], the hardest sound in Swedish, made deep in the throat.
A reported wh-question keeps the subject before the verb: var vi bodde, not var bodde vi.
After att, inte sits before the verb: att du inte kunde komma. English never moves 'not' like this.
Gott takes the neuter -t here because it describes the verb doftar, not a noun. Adverbs use the -t form: doftar gott.
Skit samma is a crude, slangy way to say 'whatever'. Keep it for casual speech only.
Som fan is a vulgar intensifier, roughly 'as hell'. Use it in casual or vulgar speech only.
Swedish stacks words into long compounds: skorstensfejarens builds from skorsten (chimney) and fejare (sweeper). The last part sets the gender.
Kan means both 'can' and 'know how to': Hon kan prata means she knows how to speak.
After var, the subclause keeps the subject before the verb: var han bor, not var bor han.
Jag vill ha en öl is blunt for ordering. Kan jag få en öl is politer when you ask for something.
Sweden is nearly cashless, so betala med kort works almost everywhere and cash is often refused.
Kanske can trigger verb-second: Kanske kommer han means maybe he comes, with the verb before the subject.
Inte follows the modal verb in a main clause: kan inte simma. The negation sits right after kan.
Inte splits the particle verb tycka om: tycker inte om. The om belongs to the verb, not a preposition.
Hur vill du betala: du works for everyone since the 1960s du-reform, strangers and bosses alike.
A frequency adverb sits right after the verb in a main clause: är alltid roligt, with alltid following är.
A time or frequency adverb goes between har and the supine: har alltid älskat, not har älskat alltid.
Fronting anything forces the verb before the subject: Redan klockan sex vaknade jag, with vaknade ahead of jag.
Swedish glues 'the' onto the noun as a suffix -et: huset = the house. There is no separate word for 'the'.
A fronted sentence adverb forces verb-second: Dessutom regnar det puts regnar before det.
Hoppas ends in -s so it looks passive, but it is active and means 'we hope': vi hoppas att.
I och med att reads word for word as 'in and with that' but simply means given that or since.
For habitual or general statements the s-passive wins: maten lagas av kocken adds -s to the verb instead of using bli.
Dit means 'to where' and marks motion: platsen dit vi reste. Där means 'where' for a static location.
